subject: How to set the number of evaluation points for posterior marginals of the Gaussian field

messages.author: 3f1b57241ff195d2
messages.subject: How to set the number of evaluation points for posterior marginals of the Gaussian field
parts:
Hi!

Is it possible to control the number of evaluation points for the posterior marginals of the underlying field?

Let inla.object be the output of inla()   [In case you find it relevant, I am using the spde approach on a Cox process in this particular case]

I am then running 

res = inla.spde2.results(inla.object,"...",spde) 

and then I extract the marginals by

res$marginals.values[[k]] for each k in the Gaussian field.

However, I am only getting 35 evaluation points here. Is there a setting which can give me more?

I want more as I would like to exp-transform these Gaussian marginals (using inla.tmarginal, I guess).

I highly appreciate any pointers in the right direction.

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to set the number of evaluation points for posterior marginals of the Gaussian field
parts:
Hi, the current setting is to use 35 for 'huge' models (graph->n >
50E3) and 75 for smaller models. (this change were made in mid-january
this year). there is no computational costs involved, really, its just
a matter of reducing the storage. 

there is currently no option to disable this reduction from 75 to 35,
but if you really need one, I can add always add it. 

H

Thank you for the quick reply and clarification. 

To achieve what I wanted,I took another approach, using inla.posterior.sample, but I think an optional number of evaluation points would be a very useful option anyway.

Unless I have misunderstood something, when using inla.tmarginal or say inla.emarginal with a transformation function, only these few supplied values are being used in the computation, am I right? 
Thus, the output may not be very accurate if the transformation function is highly nonlinear and only 35 points are being used. I guess one can always manually interpolate between the supplied evaluation points to get a finer grid, but letting inla spit out a larger number of values initially (if requested) seems like a smoother way.

- Martin

On Thu, 2016-03-10 at 13:03 -0800, Martin Jullum wrote:

> Unless I have misunderstood something, when using inla.tmarginal or
> say inla.emarginal with a transformation function, only these few
> supplied values are being used in the computation, am I right? 
> Thus, the output may not be very accurate if the transformation
> function is highly nonlinear and only 35 points are being used. I
> guess one can always manually interpolate between the supplied
> evaluation points to get a finer grid, but letting inla spit out a
> larger number of values initially (if requested) seems like a
> smoother way.

if this is about transforming hyperparameters, then *always* start from
the marginals on the internal scale. they are constructed to be
Gaussian like and well behaved. although the marginal you put it, is
interpolated (using inla.smarginal), there are cases where you can
loose accuracy mapping between different parametersisations. 


here is an example computing the posterior for the standard deviation.
in general 'si' would be more accurate than 's1' but not in this case.
the marginal in internal scale is found as
r$internal.marginals.hyperpar

> r = inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y=0))
> m1 = r$marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
> mi = r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
> s1 = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/sqrt(x), m1)
> si = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/sqrt(exp(x)), mi)
> plot(s1)
> lines(si)


H

--

parts:
ohh, that was quite a difference. Intuitively, I would bet on A, as one
avoid the transformation. since exp(x) is kind of exploding, then
you're right, the tail behaviour would dominate here. Also I would
check that the density does indeed goes to zero. in the function
'inla.smarginal' you can also extrapolate, but it do that at linear
rate in log-scale. unfortunately, the tail behaviour might not be so
accurate, in the sense that the rate is postulated not necessarily
computed. 

In general, I am a bit (or even more than a bit) sceptical to E()
values when tail dominate, like the E(precision) is often meaningless
due to the tail, which in fact boil down to that squared error does not
make sense. E(log(prec)) is usually much much better. (its like why
should be care of an unbiased estimator for variance? the distribution
is skewed hence I do not care about E(variance)?)

Maybe I would consider to use quantiles instead, f.ex  median. from the
marginal you can get the median, and then exp(median) is the median in
the new scale. much less mess and hopefully more stable with less tail
influence. 

H
